title: Fixing the PR Bottleneck — Matt Pocock, AIHero
talk_summary: Matt Pocock argues the PR bottleneck is fixed by layering cheap deterministic checks, then automated review, then human review, and by treating human review as feedback into the system that produces code. Key mechanisms: keep coding standards out of the implementer's context and put them in a separate reviewer sub-agent that commits fixes, and run retrospectives over PRs/sessions to add checks and standards so the same comment is never made twice.

takeaways.technique: Separate reviewer sub-agent with its own context for coding standards
takeaways.what_they_do: Coding standards live in coding-standards.md and are applied only by a review sub-agent with its own context window; the implementer is not loaded with standards because implementation is already overloaded with explore/change/debug.

takeaways.technique: Reviewer commits fixes instead of commenting
takeaways.what_they_do: The automated reviewer's default output is commits that fix what it finds; it only comments when it has a genuine question, so the human reviews a clean artifact rather than a pile of comments.
takeaways.evidence_quote: The reviewer should commit. It should make fixes... the default should be commits.

takeaways.technique: Harden automated checks against lying tests
takeaways.what_they_do: Treat green CI as untrusted: hunt tautological tests, structure-sensitive tests that read source files, and mocked-away failure modes; push tests to exercise deep-module interfaces instead of implementation details.

takeaways.technique: Retro skill that converts review comments into checks and standards
takeaways.what_they_do: A retrospective skill ingests a session or a week of PRs/reviews and proposes new automated checks, coding-standards.md updates, navigation pointers in agents.md, and token-economy/bloat fixes to steering files.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you never want to write the same comment twice... It will suggest automated checks and coding standards to make the next one better.

takeaways.technique: One-way vs two-way door triage with merge-danger summary
takeaways.what_they_do: Each PR is classified by reversibility and blast radius, and the PR body ends with a merge-danger summary so reviewers spend effort only on one-way doors and localized-risk changes get light review.
takeaways.evidence_quote: some reviews are more important than others... is it a one-way door or is it a two-way door?

takeaways.what_they_do: PR descriptions replace prose with mermaid/UML diagrams and small pseudocode summaries so a reviewer grasps what changed and why in seconds.
takeaways.evidence_quote: dispenses with most text and shows things to you in images and diagrams instead... make understanding the why as fast as possible
